---
title: "Ex3 - Getting and Knowing your Data (Occupation) - Solutions"
output: html_document
---

This time we are going to pull data directly from the internet.
Special thanks to: https://github.com/justmarkham for sharing the dataset and materials.

### Step 1. Import the necessary libraries

```{r step1, message=FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
```

### Step 2. Import the dataset from this [address](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/justmarkham/DAT8/master/data/u.user).

### Step 3. Assign it to a variable called users and use the 'user_id' as index

```{r}
users <- read_delim("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/justmarkham/DAT8/master/data/u.user",
                    delim = "|")

# tibbles have no index; we keep user_id as the first column, which plays that role.
# (With a base data.frame you could use: tibble::column_to_rownames(users, "user_id"))
users <- users |> relocate(user_id)
```

### Step 4. See the first 25 entries

```{r}
print(head(users, 25), n = 25)
```

### Step 5. See the last 10 entries

```{r}
tail(users, 10)
```

### Step 6. What is the number of observations in the dataset?

```{r}
nrow(users)
```

### Step 7. What is the number of columns in the dataset?

```{r}
# user_id is a regular column here, so there is one more column than in pandas
ncol(users)
```

### Step 8. Print the name of all the columns.

```{r}
names(users)
```

### Step 9. How is the dataset indexed?

```{r}
# the "index" is the user_id column
users$user_id |> head(20)
```

### Step 10. What is the data type of each column?

```{r}
sapply(users, class)

# or
glimpse(users)
```

### Step 11. Print only the occupation column

```{r}
users$occupation |> head(20)

# or, keeping it as a tibble
users |> select(occupation)
```

### Step 12. How many different occupations are in this dataset?

```{r}
n_distinct(users$occupation)

# or by counting the unique values
# users |> count(occupation) |> nrow()
```

### Step 13. What is the most frequent occupation?

```{r}
# Because "most" is asked
users |>
  count(occupation, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(occupation)

# or, to have the top 5
# users |> count(occupation, sort = TRUE) |> head(5)
```

### Step 14. Summarize the DataFrame.

```{r}
# Notice: character columns only show their length and class
summary(users)
```

### Step 15. Summarize all the columns

```{r}
# converting the text columns to factors makes summary() count the categories
users |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor)) |>
  summary()
```

### Step 16. Summarize only the occupation column

```{r}
summary(as.factor(users$occupation))

users |>
  summarise(count = n(),
            unique = n_distinct(occupation),
            top = names(which.max(table(occupation))),
            freq = max(table(occupation)))
```

### Step 17. What is the mean age of users?

```{r}
round(mean(users$age))
```

### Step 18. What is the age with least occurrence?

```{r}
users |>
  count(age) |>
  filter(n == min(n)) # 7, 10, 11, 66 and 73 years -> only 1 occurrence
```
